newsitem.title: USA: US foreign crudes quiet, but Cusiana heard done.
newsitem.headline: US foreign crudes quiet, but Cusiana heard done.

text.p: A mostly quiet foreign crude scene at the U.S. Gulf Coast was stirred by talk Colombia's state oil company Ecopetrol successfully moved another cargo of its light sweet Cusiana crude on Wednesday, traders said.
Ecopetrol's cargo for loading in the August 29 to September 2 period was heard done at minus 82 cents to September West Texas Intermediate/Cushing. The buyer was said to be a U.S. refiner.
According to traders, Ecopetrol now has just one cargo in August left to move, the one for loading August 19-23.

Colombia figured highly in traders' minds Wednesday following Occidental Petroleum's force majeure declaration Tuesday on the 180,000 barrel per day output at the Cano Limon field following a string of rebel bombings on the pipeline that connects the oil field to world markets.
Some traders were boldly predicting Gulf Coast refiners who run Cano Limon, including two majors, were on the verge of cutting runs due to the delays in deliveries.
But most players dismissed such talk as nonsense, saying refining economics on the Gulf Coast's "Refinery Row" were just too attractive to cut runs.

Instead, players who refine Cano would be wiser to look for alternatives like Angolan Cabinda or Mexican Olmeca crudes, according to most traders. But they allowed that securing prompt cargoes of Cano alternatives was a project with an uncertain outcome.

Such players might also draw down inventories and gamble that they will begin receiving their Cano cargoes sooner rather than later, though no one could say for sure how long the force majeure might stay in effect.
One player offering Brent for end-August delivery at minus 25 cents to WTI/Cushing appeared prepared to jack up the price in connection with the Cano Limon crisis.

But players on the bidding side of the market divide were unwilling to conclude yet that Colombia's woes with its leftist guerrillas had the critical mass to upset the entire foreign crude market at the Gulf Coast.
